title: CPSC 541 - Chapter 3: Good Practices for Requirements Engineering

questions.question: Requirements development consists of which four major activities?
questions.explanation: Chapter 3 expands on the four requirements development activities: elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation.

questions.question: The four requirements development activities should always be completed in a strict sequence, with one phase completely finished before the next begins.
questions.explanation: The process should be iterative, incremental, and interleaved rather than strictly sequential.

questions.question: Which description best matches an iterative requirements process?
options: Requirements are written once and never revisited
Teams repeatedly revisit and refine earlier work as new information is discovered
Requirements work starts only after implementation
Each activity is performed by a completely separate team
questions.explanation: The slides show requirements work cycling back to clarify, rewrite, correct, and re-evaluate earlier information.

questions.question: What is one purpose of defining the requirements development process before beginning elicitation?
options: To define the steps and activities the team will use to develop requirements
To write all test cases immediately
To guarantee requirements will never change
questions.explanation: A good practice is to define the requirements development process, including its steps and activities.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a vision and scope document?
options: To define project objectives, boundaries, and focus
To list every future test case
To document only user interface colors
questions.explanation: The vision and scope document defines objectives, sets project boundaries, and helps keep the project focused.

questions.question: Which factors can help distinguish different user classes? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The slides list all of these as useful characteristics for identifying different user classes.

questions.question: Why is identifying user classes important during elicitation?
options: Different groups may use the system differently and have different needs
Every user always wants exactly the same thing
It determines which programming language must be used
It eliminates the need for customer representatives
questions.explanation: Different user classes can have different roles, goals, skills, and usage patterns, so their requirements may differ.

questions.question: What is a product champion?
options: The developer who writes the most code
A representative of a user class who speaks and may make decisions on behalf of that group
A project manager responsible only for budget
A customer who uses the system once
A tester responsible for all acceptance testing
A person who approves every software change
questions.explanation: Product champions represent user classes, speak for them, and generally make a long-term commitment to the project.

questions.question: A product champion is usually expected to have a long-term commitment to the project.
questions.explanation: The slides distinguish product champions by their ongoing representation and long-term project involvement.

questions.question: How does a focus group differ from a product champion?
options: Focus groups are typically short-term participants who describe functionality and quality needs
Focus groups have authority over the entire project
Focus groups replace all user classes
Focus groups are used only after deployment
questions.explanation: Focus groups provide input about functionality and quality needs but usually have a shorter-term commitment than product champions.

questions.question: Use cases primarily help identify:
options: Tasks users need to accomplish, their goals, and user-system interactions
questions.explanation: Use cases describe tasks, goals, purposes, and interactions between users and the system.

questions.question: Which of the following can be considered system events? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The slides identify external signals and data, temporal events, and business events such as customer calls or inventory changes.

questions.question: Why identify system events and responses during elicitation?
options: To understand how the system should behave when particular stimuli or events occur
To choose source code naming conventions
To create the final database implementation
questions.explanation: System events and responses help reveal required system behavior.

questions.question: What is a requirements workshop?
options: A collaborative session where analysts and users discuss requirements and develop draft material
questions.explanation: Workshops promote collaboration between analysts and users through discussion and draft requirements work.

questions.question: Observing users performing their current work can help analysts understand the context for a new system.
questions.explanation: Observation can reveal current tasks, workflows, and data flows that may not be fully captured through interviews alone.

questions.question: What useful information can be captured by observing users?
questions.explanation: Observation helps establish context and can reveal actual data flow and work practices.

questions.question: Why should analysts examine problem reports from an existing system?
options: Problems and requested enhancements can reveal requirements for the new system
They are only useful to testers
They eliminate the need for user input
They guarantee the new system will have no defects
questions.explanation: Problems with the old system and previously requested enhancements can provide valuable requirements information.

questions.question: What does requirements reuse mean in Chapter 3?
options: Looking for relevant requirements from previous projects or existing products that may apply again
Copying all requirements from any old project without review
Using the same project manager on every project
questions.explanation: Reuse means identifying applicable similarities with previous projects or products rather than starting from nothing.

questions.question: What is a context diagram used for during requirements analysis?
options: To show the system's environment, boundaries, and interfaces
questions.explanation: A context diagram provides a high-level view of the system, its environment, boundaries, and external interfaces.

questions.question: A prototype of a user interface can be useful because it gives users something tangible to react to and provide feedback on.
questions.explanation: The slides specifically describe UI prototypes as a way to obtain feedback on a tangible representation.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a technical prototype?
options: To explore the feasibility of potential technical problem areas
To create the final product immediately
questions.explanation: Technical prototypes help determine whether difficult or uncertain aspects of a proposed solution are feasible.

questions.question: Why are requirements prioritized during analysis?
options: To allocate requirements to releases and adjust to changing resources, needs, goals, or market conditions
To ensure every requirement has equal importance
questions.explanation: Prioritization helps decide what should be implemented first and supports adjustments when circumstances change.

questions.question: Requirements modeling can help reveal which types of problems? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Abstract and rigorous models can expose incompleteness, inconsistency, conflicts, and unclear relationships.

questions.question: During analysis, teams should identify interfaces with other systems and requirements that affect other subsystems.
questions.explanation: The slides include identification of external interfaces and requirements allocated to other subsystems as analysis activities.

questions.question: What is one major goal of requirements specification?
options: To create documentation that is consistent, accessible, and reviewable
To reduce the number of stakeholders
questions.explanation: Specification should produce requirements documentation that can be consistently understood, accessed, and reviewed.

questions.question: What kind of document template is suggested in the slides for software requirements specifications?
questions.explanation: The slides explicitly mention adopting an SRS template such as IEEE 830.

questions.question: Why should the source or origin of a requirement be recorded?
options: To justify why the requirement exists and support future clarification
To determine who should write the source code
questions.explanation: Recording sources helps explain the requirement's presence and allows analysts to return to the originator when clarification is needed.

questions.question: Why should individual requirements have unique identifiers?
options: To support traceability and requirements management
To make requirements harder to read
To identify the programmer who wrote them
questions.explanation: Unique IDs help trace, manage, reference, and track individual requirements.

questions.question: According to the slides, business rules should generally be kept separate from the SRS because:
options: They can exist beyond the scope of a single software project
questions.explanation: Business rules often exist independently of a particular software application or project.

questions.question: Which of the following are quality attributes emphasized in the specification section? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The slides list performance, efficiency, reliability, robustness, and usability as important quality attributes.

questions.question: What is one validation practice described in Chapter 3?
questions.explanation: Validation includes formal and informal inspection of requirements documents.

questions.question: What distinguishes a formal requirements inspection?
options: It is a rigorous examination involving people with different perspectives and expertise
It is performed only by one developer
It focuses only on programming style
questions.explanation: Formal inspection is a structured review involving multiple perspectives and areas of expertise.

questions.question: Which activities are associated with defining test cases during validation? Select all that apply.
options: Review test cases with customers or users
Trace test cases back to the specification
questions.explanation: The slides connect test cases to expected behavior, customer review, traceability, and acceptance criteria.

questions.question: Requirements management primarily focuses on:
options: Controlling and tracking changes to established requirements
questions.explanation: Once requirements are established, management is largely about controlling and tracking change.

questions.question: What are the three main steps mentioned for a change control process?
questions.explanation: The slide describes a change control process consisting of proposal, analysis, and resolution.

questions.question: What is a Change Control Board (CCB)?
options: A small, competent, empowered group that decides how proposed changes should be handled
questions.explanation: The CCB evaluates and makes decisions about proposed requirements changes.

questions.question: What does change impact analysis evaluate? Select all that apply.
options: Other artifacts affected by the change
Only whether the customer likes the idea
Potential effects on related system elements
questions.explanation: Impact analysis looks at the scope of the proposed change, related artifacts, effort, cost, and broader effects.

questions.question: Why are baseline and version control important in requirements management?
options: They help distinguish release baselines and previous versus current requirement versions
They remove the need for history
questions.explanation: Baseline and version control help teams know which set of requirements belongs to which release and what changed between versions.

questions.question: A requirements change history should allow the team to know which four things?
options: What changed, when it changed, who changed it, and why
Who programmed it, where they worked, when they arrived, and how much they earn
Which server, database, framework, and language were used
Which user, computer, browser, and operating system were involved
What was tested, who tested, which IDE, and which compiler
questions.explanation: The slides specifically say a change history should capture the what, when, who, and why.

questions.question: Which sequence contains valid requirements change statuses from the slides?
questions.explanation: The transcript and slides identify proposed, approved, implemented, and verified as example change states.

questions.question: What does requirements volatility measure?
options: The rate at which requirements are changing
questions.explanation: Volatility refers to how frequently or rapidly requirements change.

questions.question: High requirements volatility can indicate which possible problems? Select all that apply.
options: Possible instability in the requirements process
questions.explanation: The slides mention poor understanding, weak scope definition, business dynamics, and politics as possible causes of high volatility.

questions.question: Why might a requirements management tool be useful?
options: Automation can reduce repetitive work and support tracking, versioning, and traceability tasks
It removes the need for requirements analysts
It eliminates the need for requirements
It automatically decides which features are correct
questions.explanation: The slides note that tools can eliminate drudgery and help perform requirements management tasks more effectively.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a requirements traceability matrix?
options: To connect requirements to design, code, and tests
To replace the source code repository
questions.explanation: A traceability matrix links requirements through later development artifacts.

questions.question: Which benefits can a traceability matrix provide? Select all that apply.
options: Ensure required functionality is not missed
Connect requirements to code and tests
Help prevent unwanted features from appearing
Show how requirements flow through development
questions.explanation: Traceability helps ensure required work is implemented and prevents functionality with no requirement justification from being added.

questions.question: A developer adds a feature that cannot be traced back to any approved requirement. What problem can traceability help reveal?
questions.explanation: Traceability can expose features that were added without an approved requirement.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the overall Chapter 3 process?
options: Develop requirements iteratively through elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation, then manage changes in a controlled and traceable way
Write requirements once, freeze them, then begin coding
Let customers define all technical design choices
Skip analysis and rely on prototypes
Complete all programming before validating requirements
questions.explanation: Chapter 3 presents requirements engineering as an iterative development process followed by disciplined requirements management.
